title: Dave Returns

jokes.text: Tom's list of nicknames for Ann: 'Boo Boo Bear, Cookie Tush, Winnie the Boo, Lady Presh Presh, Annberry Sauce, Annie Get Your Boo, Tommy's Girl, Annie Banannie'
jokes.setup: Ann asks what Tom called her, expecting one embarrassing nickname
jokes.punchline: Tom reveals an entire arsenal of increasingly absurd nicknames, each worse than the last, rattling them off without shame
jokes.explanation: The escalating list is perfectly character-specific to Tom — his over-the-top romantic delusion is baked into every syllable. 'Cookie Tush' and 'Annie Get Your Boo' are genuinely inventive wordplay. The rapid-fire delivery with no shame is peak Tom Haverford. Ann's horrified 'Wow. Just right out the gate' reaction adds a perfect straight-man beat. Earns its high score because the nicknames themselves are funny as individual items AND as a cumulative escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey there, sugar plum. How was your day?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Sugar plum? We went out ONE time!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, and it was magical, honeybun. I'm already picking out baby names.

jokes.text: Tom attempts some kind of romantic physical move on Ann in the office; Ann shuts it down: 'Is this not one of those? I might have misread the vibe.'
jokes.setup: Tom does something physically presumptuous (implied attempt at a kiss or embrace) in a clearly inappropriate workplace context
jokes.punchline: 'I might have misread the vibe' — Tom's breezy, unbothered self-assessment of a deeply awkward moment
jokes.explanation: 'I might have misread the vibe' is a beautifully deadpan understatement — the casual, almost philosophical delivery of someone who has absolutely zero self-awareness. It's pure Tom character comedy and lands well as a quick beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so I've come up with some nicknames for you. You can pick your favorite.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: There's 'Ann Perkins,' classic. 'A-Perk,' fun and zippy. 'Annie Oakley,' strong and independent.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: 'The Ann-vernator,' Terminator reference. 'Ann-tastic,' self-explanatory.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: 'Annabelle,' feminine and mysterious. 'Ann-athon,' because you're a strong woman athlete.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: 'Ann-imal,' because you're wild. 'Ann-droid,' because you're perfect and mechanical.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: 'The Annnette,' fancy. 'Ann-credible,' like Incredible, but with Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And my personal favorite... 'Tommy's Girl.'

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Absolutely not.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Can I at least change my Facebook status to "in a relationship"?' / Ann: 'Definitely not.' / Tom: '"It's complicated"?' / Ann: 'Whatever.' / Tom: 'Am I in a relationship?' / [scene cut] / Tom talking head: 'It's complicated.'
jokes.setup: Tom negotiates the terms of his relationship status on Facebook after Ann tells him to keep things secret
jokes.punchline: The talking-head cut confirms his Facebook status is literally 'It's complicated' — the show uses the mockumentary format as the punchline delivery mechanism
jokes.explanation: Exceptionally well-structured joke that uses the mockumentary format as the punchline. The escalating negotiation (relationship → complicated → am I in a relationship?) builds to a perfectly timed cut where the talking-head itself IS the answer. The form and content are unified. Economy is near-perfect — every exchange has a function. One of the episode's best-crafted moments.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, I've been thinking about us, and I realized something important.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my god, Tom, what is it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I want to take our relationship to the next level. I got us matching velvet tracksuits.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, no—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, there's more. I rented us a party bus for next Saturday, hired a DJ, and I'm going to propose to you in front of everyone at the Sweetums factory.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, I'm trying to tell you I'm pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know! That's why the tracksuits are stretchy.

jokes.text: Ben references Dead Poets Society to the police chief — 'Oh, Captain, my Captain' — then when asked 'You getting weird already?' he says 'Nope. I'm good.'
jokes.setup: Ben is nervously trying to impress a police chief he is afraid of, and reaches for a cultural reference
jokes.punchline: The reference lands completely flat; Ben's 'Nope. I'm good' is a transparent lie delivered by someone who is clearly not good
jokes.explanation: Competent character comedy — Ben's awkward nerd energy trying to impress authority is well-established. The Dead Poets Society reference is mildly funny because it's such a weird choice. 'Nope. I'm good' as immediate denial is a solid beat. Functional but not especially inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm really embarrassed about what happened.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You should be.

jokes.text: Leslie talking head: 'Ben is really nervous because he is afraid of cops.' Ben: 'I'm not afraid of cops. I have no reason to be. I never break any laws, ever.' Cut back to Leslie. Ben talking head: 'Because I'm deathly afraid of cops.'
jokes.setup: Leslie states Ben is afraid of cops; Ben immediately and emphatically denies it
jokes.punchline: Ben's own talking head immediately confirms Leslie was right: 'Because I'm deathly afraid of cops' — the escalation from 'afraid' to 'deathly afraid' is a bonus
jokes.explanation: Classic mockumentary structure used with precision: denial immediately undercut by the subject themselves. The upgrade from 'afraid' to 'deathly afraid' in Ben's confession is a smart escalation that rewards close listening. Well-executed Parks format comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So are we together or not?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's complicated.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Well, mo' money, mo' problems. That's what I always say.' / Chief: 'How about mo' money, more protective Kevlar vests that save lives?' / Leslie: '(STAMMERING) Sometimes, I say that, too.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to deflect the chief's concern about Newport donations with a Notorious B.I.G. reference
jokes.punchline: The chief immediately turns it into a sensible policy argument; Leslie's desperate stammered agreement is the laugh
jokes.explanation: Leslie's casual deployment of rap slang followed by immediate backpedaling when caught is very characteristic. The chief's pivot is unexpectedly earnest and sharp. The stammered '…Sometimes, I say that, too' is the real punchline — Leslie's political instinct to agree with everything overriding her dignity.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know, like in Die Hard, when Alan Rickman is up on the building? That's a movie reference. Die Hard. It came out in 1988. Bruce Willis is in it. There's explosions. And, um, he's trying to save his wife. Her name is Holly. Holly Gennaro Willis. Actually it's just Holly Gennaro in the movie, because she goes by her maiden name at work, which is actually pretty progressive for an action film from the late eighties.

jokes.text: Tom announces a flesh-eating virus is 'going around' for dramatic effect, then reveals: 'Yeah. It's called music. And there's only one way to get a vaccine. And that is to play it.'
jokes.setup: Tom creates alarm by announcing a serious health crisis in the office
jokes.punchline: The 'flesh-eating virus' is a metaphor for his song; the 'vaccine' is performing it — a comically over-inflated analogy for a campaign jingle
jokes.explanation: Tom's dramatic self-importance about a campaign song being like a medical emergency is solid absurdist character comedy. The misdirection works — the setup genuinely reads as a real announcement before the twist. The vaccine metaphor is a bit overwrought but that's the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm not afraid of cops. I respect the law. I follow the rules. There's no logical reason for me to be afraid of them.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. When I was twelve, Officer Daniels told me my bike was stolen, and I cried for three hours.

jokes.text: Jerry is eating during a meeting. Tom: 'Jerry, if you're eating, you're not listening.' Jerry: 'Thanks, babe.'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to run a serious meeting and calls out Jerry for eating
jokes.punchline: Jerry absentmindedly thanks Tom with 'babe,' implying he thought it was Ann speaking — a double joke that also catches Tom off guard given the secret relationship
jokes.explanation: A two-layer joke — Jerry's obliviousness and the ironic use of 'babe' toward Tom (who is desperately trying to keep his relationship with Ann secret). The word 'babe' is doing a lot of work in two syllables. Excellent economy. The rewatch value is high because the layering becomes clearer on second viewing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It was all good just a week ago.

dialogue.speaker: Police Chief
dialogue.line: That's not how the quote goes.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know, I know. I was just... riffing. You know, like Biggie would have wanted.

jokes.text: Tom: 'It's kind of like We Are the World, except I actually think it could have a real impact on society.'
jokes.setup: Tom describes his campaign jingle as being in the vein of We Are the World
jokes.punchline: The 'except' implies We Are the World had no real impact — a staggeringly arrogant dismissal of one of the most famous charity songs ever, delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical — the entire joke is compressed into the word 'except.' Tom's oblivious grandiosity is at its peak here. The implication (We Are the World = limited impact, Tom's jingle = real impact) is so absurd it lands hard. Economy score of 9 is deserved: maximum funny per word. Very quotable as a standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know what, I think you police officers are really great. You put your lives on the line every single day, and—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, no.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: —especially after 9/11—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben!

jokes.text: Ron (deadpan): 'Just say your piece, son.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just rambled through an incoherent virus/vaccine metaphor about his song
jokes.punchline: Ron cuts through all of it with one flat, paternal command
jokes.explanation: Economical Ron Swanson at his best — five words that cut through Tom's nonsense with fatherly exasperation. The 'son' is particularly choice, given Ron's relationship with Tom. The laugh comes from the contrast between Tom's elaborate setup and Ron's total dismissal of the theatrics.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So there's this flesh-eating virus, right? And it's like... it's like a home invader. Except the home is your body, and the invader is a virus. So you gotta kick it out. But you can't really kick a virus because it's invisible. So maybe you use a gun? A really tiny gun?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, no, wait. The virus is more like a bad roommate. A bad roommate that eats your flesh. Who does that? What roommate eats flesh? That's just... that's crazy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I lost the metaphor, didn't I? I definitely lost it.

jokes.text: Tom explains he was originally in charge of hot dogs at the barbecue fundraiser: 'I dropped them all. All of them. Like, 1,000.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains why writing the song is so important to him
jokes.punchline: The revelation that he dropped 1,000 hot dogs — the specificity of the number and the flat delivery make it funnier than a vague admission would be
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '1,000' hot dogs is the engine of the joke — it escalates from 'dropped some hot dogs' to a logistical catastrophe. Tom's earnest motivation from such a ridiculous failure is on-brand. Solid beat.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Our campaign song is like We Are the World, except We Are the World actually made a difference.

jokes.text: Tom mentions DoubleTime Studio on 'Liondale Road'; Ron immediately asks 'You know the one?' / Tom: 'No.' — Ron pretending not to know the studio where he secretly records
jokes.setup: Tom names the studio where Duke Silver (Ron's secret musical alter ego) records his albums
jokes.punchline: Ron's perfectly casual 'No' — a blatant lie delivered with complete deadpan conviction by a man who obviously knows the studio intimately
jokes.explanation: The Duke Silver running gag is one of Parks and Rec's great recurring bits, and this is a tight execution. The setup is natural, and Ron's monosyllabic 'No' while clearly lying is perfectly in character — the most economical possible delivery of a Duke Silver joke. Rewatch bonus because fans of the show get the full weight of Ron's elaborate deception.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was in charge of the budget for the entire campaign.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We spent $847,000.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I have no idea where any of it went.

jokes.text: Tom adds: 'You could not keep it together in there.' / Chris's response: 'I know. I'm sorry. But I'm fine now. As long as we can get out of here as quickly as possible and never come back.'
jokes.setup: Tom calls out Chris for visibly reacting to the Duke Silver studio connection
jokes.punchline: Chris claims to be fine while immediately requesting the fastest possible exit and permanent avoidance — the opposite of fine
jokes.explanation: Competent irony — Chris's denial is immediately undermined by his panicked exit request. Works as a Duke Silver gag extension but doesn't add much beyond the setup.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What are the acoustics like? Does it have isolated vocal booths? What's the mixing console setup?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't know, I've never been there.

jokes.text: Dave meets Ben and immediately gives an over-formal, oddly clinical description of his past relationship with Leslie: 'Yes, Leslie Knope is a female person with whom I was involved. We had, romantic... Romantical involvement until I relocated to San Diego. Which is... That's in California, which is southwest of here by a number of miles. So, we terminated our involvement at that time.'
jokes.setup: Dave is introduced to Leslie's new boyfriend and tries to explain his past relationship
jokes.punchline: The increasingly clinical, geographic, and bureaucratic language ('terminated our involvement,' 'southwest of here by a number of miles,' 'Romantical involvement') reveals Dave's complete inability to be casual about an awkward situation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's genuine standout moments. The escalating formality ('romantical involvement,' 'terminated our involvement,' geographic coordinates) builds a perfect comedic portrait of a cop-brained man trying to process human emotion. 'Romantical' is an inspired malapropism — almost correct but subtly off, like Dave himself. The joke earns its high scores because the character voice is completely specific and the escalation is perfectly calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Well, Leslie and I have a relationship that is... geographically situated in Pawnee, Indiana, which is in the Midwest, and our emotional connection is predicated on a series of interactions that occurred over a temporal span of several months, during which we engaged in various activities together, including but not limited to dining, conversing, and maintaining a consistent pattern of eye contact that some might characterize as romantic in nature, though I would describe it more as a sustained mutual acknowledgment of each other's existence within the same physical space.

jokes.text: Dave says he's going to 'go to the gas station and get a frozen burrito and eat it right there at that table' while Ben and Leslie are going to a nice French restaurant
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie are describing their dinner plans at a fancy restaurant; Dave has no plans
jokes.punchline: Dave's plan — a gas station frozen burrito eaten alone at a gas station table — is delivered with the same flat affect as a normal dinner plan, making his loneliness both funny and a little sad
jokes.explanation: The specificity ('right there at that table') elevates this from a generic sad-bachelor joke to something character-specific. Dave is so literal and unbothered that his deadpan delivery of his own loneliness becomes funnier than any self-aware complaint would be. The contrast with the French restaurant is perfectly set up by the scene structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I'll be at Applebee's with my ex-wife arguing about whose turn it is to pay for the bloomin' onion.

jokes.text: Leslie invites Dave to join their dinner, and Ben says 'I shouldn't have invited him. I'm sorry.' / Ben: 'Oh, no, no. No, that's okay.'
jokes.setup: Leslie impulsively invites her ex to dinner with her current boyfriend
jokes.punchline: Ben's immediate gracious acceptance followed by his private admission that it is very much not okay — the politeness-vs.-reality gap
jokes.explanation: Standard sitcom cringe setup — ex invited to dinner — executed with basic competence. Ben's mild-mannered acceptance is true to his character but doesn't reach the level of the better jokes in this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Double endorsement? That's like 'Double Impact' with Jean-Claude Van Damme!

jokes.text: Leslie's campaign description: 'Ooh, that sounds like an Ashley Judd movie.'
jokes.setup: Leslie describes getting two endorsements as a 'double endorsement'
jokes.punchline: Ben's immediate Ashley Judd comparison — oddly specific, perfectly timed, completely useless to the conversation
jokes.explanation: The unexpected specificity of 'Ashley Judd movie' is the laugh — it's a very particular cultural reference that does nothing except reveal Ben's oddly specific frame of reference. Short and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, I need your absolute discretion on something. Duke Silver is a very private part of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Duke Silver? That's awesome! Wait till I tell everyone at the party tonight about Ron Swanson's Duke Silver thing!

jokes.text: April points to graffiti on the studio: 'That's vandalism.' / Ron: 'I have a problem.'
jokes.setup: The group arrives at DoubleTime Studio and April points out graffiti on the building
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'I have a problem' — an understatement about his Duke Silver secret being in jeopardy, delivered as a measured self-assessment
jokes.explanation: Ron's measured acknowledgment of a problem threatening his secret life is compact and funny. Works as part of the Duke Silver suite of jokes but is a minor beat on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: So when you say you want to go in a more... what was the word... 'Spinergy' direction?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, Spinergy. It's like... spin meets energy.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Right, but is that a real word?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, I made it up. But it should be.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head about Duke Silver: 'From what I've heard about Duke, he's kind of a private guy. He doesn't want his nosy co-workers discussing his music with him. Or knowing that he exists.'
jokes.setup: Ron, IN his Duke Silver studio, gives a talking head about Duke Silver in third person, maintaining his double identity
jokes.punchline: 'Or knowing that he exists' — escalating from 'privacy' to complete erasure from reality, delivered as reasonable workplace policy
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect Duke Silver joke. Ron referring to himself in the third person while sitting in his own recording studio is already absurd, but 'Or knowing that he exists' escalates the request to delightful extremes. It's the funniest possible version of Ron's secrecy obsession. Character integration is a 9.5 because this joke is literally impossible without Ron's specific dual identity. Quotable as a standalone.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm sorry I told everyone about our date. I just... I couldn't help myself.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, you told the entire department within five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's because you're too attractive to keep secret. It's not my fault you're so beautiful that I had to share the good news with everyone I know.

jokes.text: April says to Ron: 'You got it, Duke.' Ron: 'Don't call me that.' April: 'I dig your groovy tunes, man.' Ron: 'Did you hear me? I said, I dig your groovy tunes, man.'
jokes.setup: April acknowledges Ron's Duke Silver identity despite his wishes; Ron shuts her down
jokes.punchline: April repeats the exact same sentence Ron just told her not to say; Ron's confused repetition of her line suggests he may be sarcastically demonstrating or is genuinely baffled
jokes.explanation: The double-repeat structure is a bit confusing in transcript form but the joke is April's cheerful defiance of Ron and Ron's exasperated echo. April's chaotic neutral energy plays well against Ron's desire for secrecy.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: So what's going on with you and Tom?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We're just friends.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Mm-hmm. And how many times a week are you sleeping together?

jokes.text: Tom to the recording engineer: 'Yo, Chuck. We're going to go ahead and play and sing at the same time.' / 'I want this to have the electricity of a live concert. So, we have to play it perfectly every time?' / Tom: 'No, Burly. Play it unperfectly.' / 'You mean, imperfectly?' / Tom: 'I mean perfectly.' / 'God, that was hot nonsense.'
jokes.setup: Tom gives contradictory directions to the studio musicians, mangling the word 'imperfectly'
jokes.punchline: 'God, that was hot nonsense' — the engineer's perfectly timed deadpan assessment of Tom's entire creative vision
jokes.explanation: 'Hot nonsense' is a genuinely great phrase — it has the right texture of someone who's heard a lot of bad ideas and found the precise language for this one. Tom's circular logic ('unperfectly'→'imperfectly'→'perfectly') is a nice absurdist spiral. The outside perspective validating the audience's read on Tom is satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie's bathroom nickname is 'The Cistern Sister.'

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Real cute.

jokes.text: Ann and Chris share a water bottle; Tom walks in and starts 'That's sweet. The two of you sharing a nice bottle of...' then realizes they told people about their date
jokes.setup: Tom walks in on what looks like an innocent moment, starts saying something nice
jokes.punchline: Tom's warm observation collapses mid-sentence when he realizes they've already shared news he explicitly asked Ann to keep secret — visual betrayal moment
jokes.explanation: The mid-sentence pivot from warmth to betrayal is a solid cringe beat. Works best visually when the bottle-sharing becomes evidence of the secret being out.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I think Leslie is amazing and I'm completely in love with her.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I said... I think Leslie is... a MENACE. To society. A total menace.

jokes.text: Tom: 'As soon as I possibly could. I texted them while we were on the date.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks when Tom told everyone about their date
jokes.punchline: Not only did he tell people immediately, he did it in real time DURING the date — a spectacular violation of the DL request
jokes.explanation: Economically devastating joke. The escalation from 'he told them' to 'he literally texted during the date' is a beautifully compressed character indictment. Tom's shamelessness is peak character. High economy score because the line is short and does enormous work.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Sorry, the bathroom situation in this building is a nightmare. Anyway, as I was saying about the budget crisis...

jokes.text: Tom: 'I'm sorry. But you are too hot to hide, Ann. This is on you.'
jokes.setup: Tom apologizes for telling everyone about the date
jokes.punchline: The apology immediately pivots to blaming Ann for being too attractive — making it her fault he couldn't keep the secret
jokes.explanation: 'You are too hot to hide, Ann. This is on you' is the rare apologetic blame-shift executed with complete confidence. It's a perfectly Tom sentence — flattery and deflection fused together. High quotability because it's short, complete, and absurd in a very specific way. One of the episode's standout lines.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That was... that was really bad. Like, genuinely one of the worst things I've ever heard. But hey, you committed to it! That takes guts. So, uh... good job?

jokes.text: Someone (likely April or Andy) asks Tom and Ann: 'When you two spoon, who spoons who?'
jokes.setup: The group has just learned Tom and Ann are dating
jokes.punchline: The immediate, deeply personal spooning question — skipping all social niceties to ask the most intimate logistical detail
jokes.explanation: The abrupt intimacy of the question is the joke — whoever asks it (likely April given her character) has no interest in small talk and goes straight to the weirdest possible question. The height differential implied between Tom and Ann makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Tom and Ann are... dating? *long pause* I need to process this information. *blinks repeatedly* That's... that's great. That's really great. *forces smile* I'm very happy for them. *jaw tightens* This is fine. Everything is fine.

jokes.text: Tom says April's audition singing was 'hilarious-ly awful-ly funny how bad that was' while trying to avoid saying it was just bad
jokes.setup: April sings terribly during auditions; Tom has to give feedback
jokes.punchline: Tom's tortured attempt to be both honest and encouraging results in 'hilarious-ly awful-ly funny' — a grammatical car crash
jokes.explanation: Tom's mangled compliment-insult is on-brand. The adverb pile-up is a nice linguistic joke that works because Tom is clearly improvising his way through the feedback.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I should probably get going. I have an early meeting tomorrow with the... parks... and the recreation... of them.

jokes.text: Ben returns from the bathroom; Leslie covers by having invented 'Whizzingham Manor' as another funny name for the bathroom
jokes.setup: Leslie and Dave are having a tense secret conversation; Ben returns from 'the whiz palace'
jokes.punchline: Leslie deflects with 'Whizzingham Manor' — a running bit about her silly bathroom euphemisms that also covers her panic
jokes.explanation: Leslie's real-time invention of 'Whizzingham Manor' is funny as an escalation of the bathroom nickname bit. The dual purpose (deflection + joke) makes it efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what's great for your voice? Hot tea with honey.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I drink it all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, it's just honey. Straight honey. But it's hot.

jokes.text: Tom tells April to 'take 15 minutes and really think about whether or not you want to be part of this' — then immediately says: 'He's a gorgeous genius, people. Just don't question his methods.'
jokes.setup: Tom kicks April out of the session after her bad singing
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately narrates his own genius to the room, referring to himself in the third person as a 'gorgeous genius' — the self-commentary makes the power play even more absurd
jokes.explanation: Tom's self-narration as 'gorgeous genius' is a great character beat. The third-person self-assessment delivered to a room full of skeptics is maximum Tom delusion.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Watch this, I'm gonna create some real rock star energy!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa! Okay, that hurt way more than I thought it would.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But check it out — I'm fine! I'm so fine! This is great!

jokes.text: Chris to Tom: 'Tom, am I to understand correctly that you are now romantically involved with Ann Perkins?' / Tom: 'Oh, are you about to give me the whole, "She's a great girl and you need to treat her right" speech? Since you guys used to date?' / Chris: 'No. But she is, and you should.'
jokes.setup: Tom pre-empts what he expects Chris's speech to be — 'she's a great girl, treat her right'
jokes.punchline: Chris denies he was going to give the speech, then immediately gives a condensed version of it anyway
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection structure — Tom accurately predicts the speech, Chris denies it, then delivers it in four words. The compression of 'No. But she is, and you should' is perfect; it's a full moral position in minimal syllables. Chris's character (earnest, unable to let things go) makes this feel earned.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm an expert at understanding women and their needs.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I make them angry all the time.

jokes.text: Chris talking head: 'I just had no idea. And so, now, I have to...' [long pause] '...adjust.'
jokes.setup: Chris discovers Tom and Ann are dating — two people from his recent past
jokes.punchline: The enormous pause before 'adjust' — all of Chris's emotional processing compressed into one painfully inadequate word, with a beat of silence doing the real heavy lifting
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best character comedy moment. The pause before 'adjust' does enormous emotional and comedic work — Chris is clearly devastated and processing something significant, and his signature optimistic euphemism ('adjust') is both deeply funny and quietly poignant. The timestamp [09:23] shows the pause is real and substantial. Character integration is a 9 because only Chris — with his forced positivity and history with both Tom and Ann — could deliver this joke. Economy is a 9.5 because one word after a long pause carries everything.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Take me out to the ball game, take me out to the crowd. Buy me some peanuts and Cracker Jacks, I don't care if I never get back. Because it's root, root, root for the home team, if they don't win it's a shame. For it's one, two, three strikes, you're out, at the old ball game. Boom.

jokes.text: 'Okay. Great talk.' — Tom's dismissal of Chris after Chris's emotional confession
jokes.setup: Chris has just had a genuine emotional moment about Tom and Ann's relationship
jokes.punchline: Tom's breezy corporate sign-off 'Great talk' as if they've just concluded a productive meeting, completely ignoring the emotional weight
jokes.explanation: 'Great talk' is a well-worn sitcom beat but works here because the contrast with Chris's genuine vulnerability is sharp. Economy is high — two words do the job completely.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so Dave wants to talk to me first, but Ben needs to talk to me second, unless Dave's thing is about the budget, in which case Ben goes first, but only if it's about the Sweetums deal, and if it's about both the budget AND Sweetums, then we do a coin flip, but only if it's heads, because tails means we go in reverse alphabetical order by first name, which would put Ben before Dave anyway, so actually that doesn't matter...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? Let's just do rock-paper-scissors. Best two out of three. Actually, best three out of five. No wait—best of seven, because seven is a lucky number, and I want to make sure we get this right.

jokes.text: At the restaurant, Dave tells Leslie: 'I'm still in love with you.' Then immediately: 'Nothing was said. Nothing was just now...'
jokes.setup: Ben has stepped away to the bathroom; Dave seizes the moment to confess his feelings
jokes.punchline: Dave immediately tries to walk back the confession with hilariously unconvincing denials: 'Nothing was said. Nothing was just now...'
jokes.explanation: The confession/immediate denial pivot is a classic cringe-comedy beat. Dave's specific inability to construct a grammatical denial ('Nothing was just now') is true to his character — he's great at police work, terrible at emotional vocabulary. Works well within the episode's stakes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I caught feelings for you. Will you be my girl?

jokes.text: Dave and Ben exchange a rapid-fire volley of competing offers to escort each other outside and talk to each other, then to Leslie, then together — devolving into an absurd negotiation.
jokes.setup: Dave wants to talk to Leslie alone; Ben wants to talk to Dave; both keep politely counter-offering
jokes.punchline: The negotiation becomes a self-parodying loop: 'I'll talk to Ben, then you, then I'll talk to you. And then you'll talk to each other, and then we'll all three talk, then.'
jokes.explanation: A finely escalated absurdist bit. Both men are too polite (and too competitive) to simply declare what they want, so the conversation calcifies into an increasingly meaningless scheduling negotiation. The final 'then' hanging at the end of the sentence is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: That's just contriring nonsense.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Do you mean 'contriving'?

jokes.text: Dave explains why he chose that moment to confess: 'Because it's accurate. And because he's not here right now, so I thought this would be a good time.'
jokes.setup: Leslie demands to know why Dave would tell her this now
jokes.punchline: Dave's reasoning is both logical and completely tone-deaf: 'Because it's accurate' (like a police report) and the tactical window of Ben being in the bathroom
jokes.explanation: 'Because it's accurate' is a gem — it applies the language of police reports and factual testimony to an emotional confession. It's exactly how a cop-brained person would justify a declaration of love. The bathroom window logic compounds the comedy. Strong character integration because only Dave would think this way.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Dave, why are you handcuffing me?

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: You were jaywalking.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was crossing at the crosswalk!

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Yeah, but you were crossing diagonally. That's two jaywalks.

jokes.text: Dave's plan: 'Okay, well, get rid of him. That's a good call.' / Leslie: 'No, bad call.' / Dave: 'That's not the call.'
jokes.setup: Dave suggests Leslie should leave Ben so he can talk to her
jokes.punchline: Dave's instant walk-back ('That's not the call') — using his police procedural vocab to process romantic rejection in real time
jokes.explanation: Dave's police-speak applied to romantic situations continues to be a reliable joke engine. 'That's not the call' is funny as a self-correction delivered in cop-report language.

dialogue.line: Obvious lies designed to make Ben look bad

jokes.text: Tom explains why he didn't wait in the rain with Ann: 'It was raining out, so I didn't want to get wet.'
jokes.setup: Context implies Tom should have done something romantic in the rain
jokes.punchline: Tom's explanation is the most obvious possible reason not to go outside — he simply didn't want to get wet, stated as if this is a complete and reasonable explanation
jokes.explanation: Competent but slight. The mundane practicality contrasting with whatever romance was expected is mildly funny. Tom's vanity (not wanting to get wet) is character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Is this rain? This is perfect. This is straight out of my playbook. Women love a guy who's wet and confused.

jokes.text: Tom talking head: 'Mine's really just a cup of honey because tea is gross.'
jokes.setup: Tom says he got hot tea with honey for his voice
jokes.punchline: Immediate correction: it's just a cup of honey because 'tea is gross' — a petulant and impractical dietary position delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: A lovely small absurdist beat — a cup of honey is both disgusting and impractical, but Tom's certainty that this is a good idea is very Tom. Economy is good; the correction ('really just a cup of honey') lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann! Ann! Hey Ann!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What, Tom?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I just wanted to say... you're looking really nice today, Ann Perkins.

jokes.text: April lets out a wild vocalization and Tom says 'I was thinking, like, a crazy rock star vibe. See where her head's at? Follow her lead.'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to reset the recording session's energy
jokes.punchline: April's random screech is immediately adopted by Tom as intentional artistic vision and presented as leadership to be followed
jokes.explanation: Tom's instant reframing of chaos as vision is a nice producer-delusion joke. April's unpredictable energy being treated as artistic direction plays well.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Why do you look so terrible?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Movies

jokes.text: Tom talking head: 'Ann's mad at me now but I have a few tricks up my sleeve. I don't want to brag, but I have a ton of experience with women being mad at me.'
jokes.setup: Tom admits Ann is angry at him
jokes.punchline: He frames his extensive history of making women angry as a SKILL rather than a character flaw — 'experience with women being mad at me' as a competitive advantage
jokes.explanation: The reframe of 'women being mad at me' as experience/expertise is a sharp ironic inversion. 'I don't want to brag' before confessing to a record of making women angry is perfectly constructed. High quotability because it's a complete, self-contained absurd thought.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Ben's not exactly a physical specimen. I mean, look at him.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Are you kidding me? Ben is incredibly attractive! He's got those piercing blue eyes, that strong jawline, and he's clearly very fit.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I don't know, he seems pretty—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Pretty what? Pretty amazing? Because he is! He's smart, he's kind, he's dedicated, and yes, he is VERY handsome. In fact, I think you're crazy for not seeing it.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I was just—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And another thing! Ben has the most incredible smile and when he laughs it's like the whole room lights up and I could listen to him talk about municipal governance all day long because he's brilliant and talented and I love him, okay?!

jokes.text: Tom (talking head): 'I think you sound like an angel and everyone else sounds like demons. I think you shouldn't whisper.' (Apparently directed at Ann)
jokes.setup: Tom is describing his approach to the individual auditions
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'feedback' is pure flattery toward Ann and brutal honesty about everyone else — 'demons' vs 'angel' — and then the absurdly useless note 'I think you shouldn't whisper'
jokes.explanation: Tom's complete inability to be a fair producer because Ann is there is a strong character joke. 'Everyone else sounds like demons' is good hyperbole. The practical note 'you shouldn't whisper' is a funny undercut after the supernatural imagery.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben is not shrimpy. He once punched a guy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we've talked about this. He was harassing a horse.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Still counts as punching someone.

jokes.text: Chris auditions by singing 'Take Me Out to the Ball Game' but progressively improvises extra lyrics: 'I just want to be at the game / I would like to eat at the game / I'd like popcorn and candy and the home team at the game'
jokes.setup: Chris is asked to sing anything he wants for the audition
jokes.punchline: He starts with 'Take Me Out to the Ball Game' but runs out of real lyrics and starts improvising earnest, increasingly mundane additions — ending with 'the home team at the game' as if it scans
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully observed character joke. Chris's relentless positivity means he commits fully to the audition even as his improvisations become increasingly desperate ('I just want to be at the game'). The escalating mundanity is perfectly calibrated — each new line is funnier than the last as he runs out of ideas. The ending 'the home team at the game' is a great closer. High character integration because Chris's sincerity in the face of failure is what makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, is that you playing the saxophone?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not. I don't play the saxophone.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But we can literally hear it right now.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's impossible. I have no idea what you're talking about.

jokes.text: Ben immediately signals the waiter: 'Here's the check, as you requested. Here's my credit card. Quick, now.'
jokes.setup: The dinner with Dave is going badly; Ben is eager to end it
jokes.punchline: Ben has pre-emptively flagged the check and has his credit card ready — the preparation suggests he's been planning the exit for some time
jokes.explanation: 'Quick, now' is a funny addition that reveals his desperation. The pre-planned exit is good character work for Ben's anxiety.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What are you even talking about right now?

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I'm just keeping it real, bro. You know, staying fresh, staying fly.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Do you actually know what any of those words mean?

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Honestly? Not really. I just hear people say them and I repeat them.

jokes.text: Ben: 'You like dessert. Why didn't you get a dessert?' / Leslie: 'Oh, dessert is overrated and gross.'
jokes.setup: Ben notices Leslie didn't order dessert despite normally loving it
jokes.punchline: Leslie's transparent lie that dessert is 'overrated and gross' — the opposite of her known position — reveals her anxiety about the Dave situation
jokes.explanation: Functional character irony — Leslie denying herself food, especially dessert, signals how stressed she is. Competent but minor beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Baby, I wrote you a song. *clears throat and starts singing off-key* You're so fine, you blow my mind, hey Tom! You're so fine, you blow my mind, hey Tom!

jokes.text: The three-way standoff about who gets to talk to whom: 'Actually, Dave, I'd like to talk to you.' / 'Well, I don't want to talk to you.' / ... escalating into a complex negotiated speaking order
jokes.setup: All three people want to have private conversations with different people at the restaurant table
jokes.punchline: The negotiation escalates into an absurd bureaucratic scheduling exercise: talk to Ben, then Leslie, then Ben talks to Leslie, then all three — resolved without anyone actually talking
jokes.explanation: The bureaucratic scheduling of emotional conversations is a great comedic concept — it reduces raw human conflict to a calendar problem. The escalation of meeting-agenda language in an emotionally charged moment is well-executed. Dave's willingness to schedule the conflict reflects his cop-brain character.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You wore me down.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's the sweetest thing you've ever said to me.

jokes.text: Tom's song 'Catch Your Dream' plays in the background; Tom bursts in: 'Stop the song! Stop the song right now. Please, stop it!' followed by a bleeped expletive from someone offscreen
jokes.setup: Tom's song is playing; Tom interrupts it dramatically
jokes.punchline: Tom's panic about his own song (which he declared to be greater than We Are the World) suggests it sounds terrible
jokes.explanation: The callback to Tom's grandiose claims about the song pays off here — his own horror at the playback is the natural consequence. Competent setup-payoff but leans on the earlier joke for its impact.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben? Why are you standing outside the bathroom?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was just... waiting.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: For what?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: For you to be done. I didn't want to interrupt.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, you have a weird thing about authority figures. You're being way too deferential.

jokes.text: Ann confrontation: 'Ann, I caught feelings for you. And I want you to be my girl. And I don't care who knows.' / Ann: 'I know you don't care, dummy. I care.'
jokes.setup: Tom makes a grand romantic declaration ending with 'I don't care who knows'
jokes.punchline: 'I know you don't care, dummy. I care.' — Ann's exasperated response cuts through Tom's romanticism by pointing out that his obliviousness is the entire problem
jokes.explanation: This is a callback that pays off the entire episode's A-plot thread about secrecy. 'I know you don't care, dummy. I care.' is both a punchline and a character truth. The word 'dummy' delivered with affectionate exasperation is perfect — it's not cruel, just perfectly accurate. Economy is a 9 because it's a six-word sentence that resolves a multi-scene conflict.

jokes.text: Tom tells Ann: 'Let's not get hung up on who wants what.' / Ann: 'You know what? I'm calling this. We're done.' / Tom: 'What about our next date?'
jokes.setup: Ann breaks up with Tom
jokes.punchline: Tom's immediate response to the breakup is to inquire about the next date — he has not processed that the relationship has ended
jokes.explanation: Tom's total failure to register the breakup is a perfect character beat. 'What about our next date?' treats the relationship's end as an administrative scheduling issue. High character integration because Tom's self-delusion is so complete he literally cannot process rejection.

jokes.text: Ann: 'If you want another date, keep walking away.' Tom watches: 'She's still walking.'
jokes.setup: Ann gives Tom an ultimatum — keep walking if you want a date
jokes.punchline: Ann keeps walking; Tom's hopeful 'She's still walking' as narration suggests he genuinely believes this is progress
jokes.explanation: 'She's still walking' as an optimistic sports commentary is a wonderful Tom moment. The gap between what's happening (she's leaving) and what Tom sees (she's earning the date) is a perfectly compressed character joke. Very economical.

jokes.text: Dave to Ben: 'I need you to know something, man to man. I still have feelings for Leslie, in a womanly fashion. And I believe she feels the same towards me, in a manly way.'
jokes.setup: Dave confronts Ben about his feelings for Leslie
jokes.punchline: Dave's careful gender-qualification of feelings — 'in a womanly fashion' and 'in a manly way' — applying police-report precision to romantic feelings to ensure legal clarity
jokes.explanation: 'In a womanly fashion' and 'in a manly way' are the episode's most specific Dave-isms — they apply his police-report precision to emotional confession in a way that's both absurd and completely character-specific. The qualifications add nothing except comic precision. High character integration because this joke only works for Dave.

jokes.text: Dave: 'I just said to you one thing. And you're contriring me.' / Ben: 'I don't think that's a word.'
jokes.setup: Dave accuses Ben of contradicting him
jokes.punchline: 'Contriring' — Dave's mangled portmanteau of 'contradicting' and possibly 'contriving' — and Ben's dry correction
jokes.explanation: 'Contriring' is a great word-invention joke — Dave's vocabulary falls apart under emotional pressure. Ben's flat 'I don't think that's a word' is the perfect straight-man response. Both characters are well-served.

jokes.text: Ben refuses to give his blessing for Dave to pursue Leslie: 'I think that that's reasonable.' / Dave: 'Okay. Okay, and I want to thank you. I want to thank you for having this talk with me, man.' / Ben: 'Oh, well, thank you. Thank you very much.'
jokes.setup: Ben has firmly shut down Dave's request; Dave thanks him warmly
jokes.punchline: Both men end up thanking each other profusely for a conversation in which one refused the other's request — the politeness ritual makes the conflict absurdly civil
jokes.explanation: The mutual thanks exchange after a confrontational refusal is absurdly Midwestern in the best way. Both characters' politeness overriding the awkwardness of the situation is gently funny.

jokes.text: Dave handcuffs Ben to something while Ben is turned away; when Leslie asks where Ben is, Dave says: 'He said, "I've got somewhere important to go, and I don't respect her as a woman." He said that. And then he acted more effeminate than he does in front of you.'
jokes.setup: Dave has handcuffed Ben and needs to explain his absence to Leslie
jokes.punchline: Dave's transparently fake account of Ben's departure — the invented quote, the unnecessary detail about acting 'more effeminate' — is so unconvincing it's funnier than any plausible lie would be
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'He said that' after an obviously fabricated quote is the anchor — it's what a cop uses when writing a statement ('subject stated that...'). The detail about acting 'more effeminate than he does in front of you' is an absurd, unprompted character assassination that makes the lie worse. Dave's complete tactical confidence while telling an obviously fake story is perfectly character-specific. High quotability because 'He said that' as a certification of an invented quote is a transferable comedic construction.

jokes.text: Dave to Leslie: '[Ben] said, "I've got somewhere important to go, and I don't respect her as a woman." He said that. And then he acted more effeminate than he does in front of you.'
jokes.setup: Dave is explaining to Leslie why Ben isn't there — he left
jokes.punchline: Dave's lie is so transparently false and bizarre — Ben 'doesn't respect her as a woman' and 'acted more effeminate' — that it's instantly unbelievable and strange
jokes.explanation: Dave's improvised lie is terrible in a very specific, character-revealing way. He uses formal accusatory language ('doesn't respect her as a woman') and then adds the bizarre 'acted more effeminate' detail — which is both irrelevant and inexplicable. The lie is so bad it loops around to funny.

jokes.text: Dave is about to make his emotional speech to Leslie; his cell phone rings mid-sentence: 'Romance... (CELL PHONE RINGING)'
jokes.setup: Dave builds up to a dramatic romantic speech: '30 seconds... Okay... Romance...'
jokes.punchline: His phone rings at the exact word 'Romance' — deflating the entire buildup with perfect comedic timing
jokes.explanation: The timing of the phone interrupting at 'Romance' is structurally perfect — it's a textbook misdirection/undercut. The buildup (30 seconds... emotional... important...) makes the deflation more satisfying. Structure score is high because the timing is the entire joke and it's well-executed.

jokes.text: After the phone interruption, Leslie: 'Are you okay?' Dave: 'Yeah. I have to pee really bad, ironically.'
jokes.setup: Dave has just had his romantic moment destroyed; Leslie checks on him
jokes.punchline: 'I have to pee really bad, ironically' — the word 'ironically' applied to a full bladder is both bathetically funny and suggests Dave has some self-awareness about the romantic collapse
jokes.explanation: 'I have to pee really bad, ironically' is one of the episode's best single lines. The word 'ironically' applied to a physiological urgency is a perfect Dave-ism — it's almost the right word for the situation (the irony being that a romantic moment ends in bathroom need) but the clinical deployment is both funny and oddly poignant. High quotability.

jokes.text: Dave reveals his master plan: 'I was thinking that I would cuff him and then I could have time to speak to you. And that you would decide to be with me, and then I would come back here and we would un-cuff him together.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks what Dave was thinking when he handcuffed Ben
jokes.punchline: Dave's plan was: handcuff boyfriend → win girlfriend → un-cuff boyfriend together as a couple — the final detail of uncuffing 'together' as a romantic bonding activity is the absurdist peak
jokes.explanation: The episode's standout joke. The plan has perfect three-act structure: problem (need alone time), solution (handcuff the obstacle), resolution (un-cuff him together as a symbol of their new relationship). The detail of 'we would un-cuff him together' is the absurdist peak — it reveals Dave's cop-logic extends to imagining the most bizarrely literal romantic gesture possible. Only a police officer character with Dave's specific combination of tactical thinking and emotional obliviousness could generate this plan. This is an 8+ joke: it's the comedic equivalent of 'Snip, snap!' in its escalation logic — each beat makes internal sense within Dave's worldview while being objectively insane. Highly quotable, iconic Parks moment.

jokes.text: Nature is 'throwing Tom a bone': Tom is standing in the rain as Ann exits, invoking 'Haverford Playbook move number two. Ladies love a guy waiting for them in the rain.'
jokes.setup: Tom is outside in the rain, framing his involuntary situation as a romantic strategy
jokes.punchline: Tom's reinterpretation of being caught in the rain as 'Haverford Playbook move number two' — attributing his accidental situation to strategy
jokes.explanation: The 'Haverford Playbook' framing is a recurring Tom character element. 'Move number two' implying there's a numbered system of romantic maneuvers is funny. The gap between Tom's manufactured strategy and his dumb luck is a reliable joke engine.

jokes.text: Ron to Tom about the song: 'Leslie is going to love it. I promise.' / Tom: 'No offense, Ron, but what do you know about music?' / Ron GRUNTS
jokes.setup: Tom dismisses Ron's opinion on music; Ron is secretly Duke Silver, a noted jazz musician
jokes.punchline: Ron's response to 'what do you know about music?' is a single grunt — the funniest possible acknowledgment of Tom's ignorance coming from a professional musician who can't reveal his expertise
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy: Ron's entire response to 'what do you know about music?' is a grunt. The audience knows he's Duke Silver, making the grunt carry enormous ironic weight — he knows everything about music but cannot say so. Economy is a 10 because zero words do more work here than any line could. Character integration is a 9.5 because the joke is completely inert without knowledge of Ron's secret identity. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Leslie to Ben, after the Dave disaster: 'Let's just go home.' / Ben: 'No. We're going to Trumple's thing.' / Leslie: 'No. Let's not go there. I don't care about the endorsement.' / Ben: 'You don't care about the endorsement?' / Ben: 'Leslie, let's not let your terrible decision-making get in the way of this election.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to give up on getting the endorsement after the disastrous evening
jokes.punchline: 'Let's not let your terrible decision-making get in the way of this election' — Ben's perfectly diplomatic way of calling Leslie out while also being supportive
jokes.explanation: 'Let's not let your terrible decision-making get in the way of this election' is a great line — it simultaneously validates Leslie (she's worth fighting for) and calls her out (her decisions tonight were terrible). The framing as campaign advice rather than personal criticism is perfectly Ben.

jokes.text: Tom reveals he was waiting in the rain as a strategy but got sick: 'I was waiting outside in the rain for you. Because I thought you would come out and be like, "Oh, he's all wet. That's so romantic." But you didn't. And now I've got the sniffles.'
jokes.setup: Tom set up a romantic rainy waiting-in-the-rain scenario
jokes.punchline: Ann didn't come out, so Tom just stood there getting sick — the grand gesture deflated by reality; 'and now I've got the sniffles' as the tragic consequence
jokes.explanation: 'And now I've got the sniffles' as the tragic consequence of a romantic gambit is a good bathos joke. The specificity of 'sniffles' (not 'a cold,' not 'pneumonia' — just 'sniffles') is nicely understated.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Why do you have to be so you all the time?' / Tom: 'I'm sorry. Will you help me get out of these wet clothes?'
jokes.setup: Ann exasperatedly calls Tom out on being himself; Tom apologizes
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'apology' immediately segues into asking Ann to help him undress — the romantic implication of the wet clothes is simultaneously the apology and a new advance
jokes.explanation: Tom's apology that is also a new romantic maneuver is classic Tom Haverford — he cannot stop even while stopping. The wet clothes ask is both funny and reveals Ann's likely softening toward him.

jokes.text: Dave on Ben: 'I guess I'm just surprised that, you know, that's the guy you fell in love with. He's very... Well, he's shrimpy. And he's small.'
jokes.setup: Dave expresses surprise that Leslie's new boyfriend is Ben
jokes.punchline: 'Well, he's shrimpy. And he's small.' — Dave offers two synonyms for the same observation as if 'shrimpy' needed clarification with 'small,' delivered with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: The double-description ('shrimpy. And he's small') is a good Dave-ism — he uses the same observation twice as if the redundancy adds emphasis or precision. The delivery straight-faced assessment of Ben's physical stature is a gentle dig that works.

jokes.text: Leslie defends Ben: 'Shrimpy or not, he's smart and he's cute and he's kind and he's funny. He's got a great face and nice hair, and he's...' / Dave: 'Okay, that's... I get it. I surrender.'
jokes.setup: Dave dismisses Ben as 'shrimpy'; Leslie defends him
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defense escalates into an increasingly enthusiastic list of Ben's attributes that goes past the point of convincing Dave and into genuine gushing — Dave's 'I surrender' suggests he's overwhelmed by the volume
jokes.explanation: Leslie's overcaffeinated enthusiasm about Ben's attributes runs past the punchline point — Dave's 'I surrender' saves it. Works as a character moment about Leslie's love for Ben but not a structurally tight joke.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'A few weeks ago, a guy called me a bitch in a bowling alley, and he punched him in the face.' Dave: 'Well, good man. I mean him, for doing that. Not the guy who called you a bitch. You tell me where he is. I'll punch him, too.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is defending Ben's character with an anecdote about him punching someone
jokes.punchline: Dave, still in full cop mode, offers to also punch the person who insulted Leslie — a gallant but legally problematic offer delivered without apparent irony
jokes.explanation: Dave clarifying who he means ('him, for doing that. Not the guy who called you a bitch') before offering his own extrajudicial punch is good character comedy. A cop casually offering to punch civilians as a show of friendship is a perfect Dave moment — the protective impulse expressed through police-adjacent violence.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'A few weeks ago, a guy called me a bitch in a bowling alley, and he punched him in the face.' / Dave: 'Well, good man. I mean him, for doing that. Not the guy who called you a bitch. You tell me where he is. I'll punch him, too.'
jokes.setup: Leslie cites Ben punching someone as evidence of his protectiveness
jokes.punchline: Dave clarifies he means the puncher is the good man (not the victim), then immediately volunteers to find and punch the name-caller himself — Dave's protective law-enforcement instincts overriding his romantic defeat
jokes.explanation: Dave's 'You tell me where he is. I'll punch him, too' is a sweet beat — even after losing Leslie, his cop-protectiveness kicks in. The clarification ('not the guy who called you a bitch') is needed and also funny as Dave ensuring accurate attribution.

jokes.text: Tom announces a new song: 'The Promise of Tomorrow's Wings. It's brilliant, about a billion times better than Catch Your Dreams, which I realize now sucks ass.'
jokes.setup: Tom was just celebrating Catch Your Dreams as potentially greater than We Are the World
jokes.punchline: Tom's complete reversal — 'which I realize now sucks ass' — delivered with the same confidence as his original endorsement, as if this new opinion is equally authoritative
jokes.explanation: Tom's complete reversal of his earlier opinion with equal confidence is a nice character bit. 'Which I realize now sucks ass' as a flat reassessment is funny in its certainty.

jokes.text: Ron plays saxophone secretly in the studio; the group hears it playing on the existing recording: 'Where is that saxophone coming from? / I don't know. / I don't know the first thing about music.'
jokes.setup: Mysterious saxophone appears on the recording; Ron denies knowledge
jokes.punchline: 'I don't know the first thing about music' — Ron's denial is the episode's most elaborate Duke Silver joke; he clearly played the saxophone himself
jokes.explanation: The Duke Silver arc pays off beautifully here. Ron secretly playing saxophone on the recording and then claiming to know 'not the first thing about music' is the episode's best sustained joke payoff. The running gag has built to this moment — every denial earlier primes this final irony. Character integration is 9.5 because it's entirely Ron-specific. Works perfectly as the B-plot's emotional climax.

jokes.text: Ben at the police retirement party spontaneously lobbying cops: 'I am telling you that Leslie, in the long run, is so much better for this police department than Bobby Newport is.' (Police all yelling) 'No, no! It's paper. I was reaching for paper.'
jokes.setup: Ben (who is 'deathly afraid of cops') is at a police retirement party and apparently makes a sudden political speech that provokes the officers
jokes.punchline: 'No, no! It's paper. I was reaching for paper.' — Ben's panicked clarification that whatever he reached for was not a weapon, in a room full of armed officers he's terrified of
jokes.explanation: This is a perfect callback payoff. Ben's established terror of cops + his campaign-manager enthusiasm colliding in a room full of armed officers results in 'It's paper. I was reaching for paper.' The panic is completely in character, the callback to 'deathly afraid of cops' pays off, and the image is hilarious. One of the episode's strongest moment — the callback structure gives it extra weight.

jokes.text: Ben at the police retirement party: 'No, no! It's paper. I was reaching for paper.'
jokes.setup: Ben (who is deathly afraid of cops) reaches for something in a room full of police officers; they all react as if it's a threat
jokes.punchline: Ben has to frantically clarify he was reaching for paper — his fear of cops has created a situation where a civilian might be about to be shot for reaching for stationery
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Ben's cop phobia gag from the episode's opening. His worst fear materializes: every cop in the room reacts to his innocent gesture. 'It's paper. I was reaching for paper' is a great, panicked punchline. The callback structure works well — we've been waiting for the cop fear to come home to roost.

jokes.text: Trumple to Ben after his speech: 'Pretty sweet sauce in there, eh, Ace?' / Ben: 'What's wrong with you?' / Trumple: 'I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Trumple assesses Ben's chaotic police-bar lobbying
jokes.punchline: 'I don't know.' — Trumple's honest, unbothered admission that his own behavior is mysterious to him
jokes.explanation: Trumple's cheerful self-ignorance ('I don't know') is a good minor beat. Economy is high because two words carry a complete character admission.

jokes.text: Leslie talking head: 'Trumple gave me the endorsement, which is great. But really, the only endorsement that matters is Ben's. And I locked that sucker up a long time ago. Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm about to endorse 10 beers into my mouth because this has been an incredibly stressful evening.'
jokes.setup: Leslie wraps up the endorsement plot; the word 'endorsement' has been used throughout the episode
jokes.punchline: 'Endorse 10 beers into my mouth' — Leslie applies the campaign vocabulary ('endorse') to drinking beer, which both subverts the formal language and captures her stress perfectly
jokes.explanation: 'Endorse 10 beers into my mouth' is a genuinely great line — it takes the episode's dominant vocabulary and applies it to a completely human need for stress relief. The formality of 'endorse' against the abandon of '10 beers into my mouth' creates a perfect tonal clash. Leslie's voice is completely present. High quotability because it works as a standalone observation about stressful days.

jokes.text: Leslie (talking head, continued): 'Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm about to endorse 10 beers into my mouth because this has been an incredibly stressful evening.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been using endorsement language; she continues the metaphor
jokes.punchline: 'Endorse 10 beers into my mouth' — applying the formal political term to drinking as a stress response, with '10' as an absurd and specific quantity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines and the most quotable. 'Endorse 10 beers into my mouth' is a perfect joke: the formal political language applied to binge-drinking is absurd, the number '10' is specific and excessive, and it perfectly captures Leslie's personality (she runs everything, even her own stress response, with the language of her work). This is genuinely excellent comedy writing.

jokes.text: After Mouse Rat records, Andy announces: 'Hey, a little tradition. After Mouse Rat records, someone buys me booze. Who's it going to be?'
jokes.setup: The recording session is over
jokes.punchline: Andy has established a 'tradition' of getting free booze after recording — the word 'tradition' for a personal extraction scheme is the joke
jokes.explanation: Andy calling a self-serving behavior a 'tradition' is a small character beat. Functional but minor.

jokes.text: Tom's final apology to Ann turns into a song: 'Baby, I'm sorry for how I acted / But if you give me another chance / I could be the boo of your dreams, girl / So when you're sleeping and you're dreaming of a boo / I want that boo to be me / I want me to be that boo / So will you date me? I'm saying...'
jokes.setup: Tom promises to apologize 'no playbook, no gimmicks, just me, Tom, talking to you as a person'
jokes.punchline: He immediately breaks that promise by singing — and the lyrics are both earnest and absurd, climaxing with the circular 'I want that boo to be me / I want me to be that boo'
jokes.explanation: A perfect structural callback. Tom opened the episode with his nickname 'Boo Boo Bear' and closes it by building an entire apology song around 'boo.' His promise of 'no gimmicks' immediately broken by the most gimmicky possible apology is the joke, but the lyrics themselves earn it — 'I want that boo to be me / I want me to be that boo' is a brilliantly circular declaration that somehow makes the joke and is also sweet.

jokes.text: Ann agrees to go out with Tom: 'Dude, you wore me down. Just stop singing. Please.' / Tom: 'The four sweetest words in the English language. "You wore me down."'
jokes.setup: Ann finally agrees to date Tom out of exhaustion
jokes.punchline: Tom celebrates 'you wore me down' as the four sweetest words in the English language — reframing attrition as romance, defeat as victory
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top moments and a genuine Parks and Rec classic line. 'You wore me down' as 'the four sweetest words in the English language' is a perfect comedic inversion — romantic language reframed as siege warfare. It's completely Tom, completely true to his character, and simultaneously funny and weirdly sweet. Economy is 9.5 because five words do everything. This line should score near the top of the episode alongside the Dave handcuff plan. High rewatch bonus because it lands differently (sweeter) on second viewing.

jokes.text: Ben is waiting in line at the bar and deferring to every cop who walks up, letting them go in front of him; Leslie has to tell him: 'It feels like you're being overly respectful of all these cops, and you're letting them go in all in front of you. Why would you be standing just here?' / Ben: 'I was just checking... Get in that. Go in!'
jokes.setup: Ben is at the bar but has been unable to actually get a drink because of his cop deference
jokes.punchline: The callback to 'deathly afraid of cops' — Ben has been paralyzed at the bar, letting every officer go ahead of him, until Leslie finally pushes him forward
jokes.explanation: A clean closing callback to Ben's cop phobia. His self-deception ('I was just checking') followed by Leslie's exasperated push is a good episode-closing joke. The physical comedy of being stuck at a bar full of cops is well-imagined. Works as a closing beat that sends the episode out on Ben's defining character trait.

tmdb_overview: While trying to get an endorsement from the Chief of Police, Leslie and Ben awkwardly run into Leslie's old flame, Dave. Meanwhile, Andy and the rest of the office work on a theme song for Leslie's campaign.
insight: Dave's return sparks 45 jokes in 45 minutes—character comedy escalates past comfort zones.
